analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier and faster to approve cheaper generic versions of prescription drugs.
analysis.headline: The GAAP Act of 2000, a bipartisan bill to speed approval of lower-cost generic drugs, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug's patent nears its end, generic copies can sell for a fraction of the price. This bill closed several common ways brand-name drug makers stretch out that exclusivity: it narrowed which patents can be used to block a generic approval, stopped companies from using delay petitions to stall generic applications unless there was real scientific proof of a safety threat, allowed alternative testing to show a generic works the same as the brand drug, and sped up competition when the first generic company sits on its approval instead of selling. It died quietly in committee as the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and payers who buy prescription drugs, because earlier generic competition brings much lower prices; generic drug manufacturers, who gain faster, clearer paths to approval.

how_it_helps.text: Limits the patents a brand company can cite to block a generic application to those claiming the active ingredient itself or the drug's first approved use, curbing the practice of listing ancillary patents to keep generics off the market [S2][S3].

Provides that a citizen petition cannot delay review and approval of a generic drug application unless it shows through substantial scientific proof that approval would threaten public health and safety, preventing petitions from being used purely to buy time [S2][S3].
Broadens bioequivalence standards so a generic can qualify using comparative pharmacodynamic studies, limited confirmation studies, or in vitro methods, not only absorption tests [S2][S3].

Speeds up competition by making the 180-day first-filer exclusivity pass to the next applicant when the first company fails to market its drug, withdraws, or changes its patent certification — including as a result of a settlement or loss in patent litigation [S2][S3].
Expresses the sense of Congress that generics should be made more available and accessible to reduce health care costs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose patents and procedural tools for delaying generic competition would be narrowed, and whose revenue from extended exclusivity periods would shrink.

drawbacks.text: Brand manufacturers argue that patent-protected exclusivity is what funds research into new medicines, and a bill that trims those protections risks reducing the incentive to develop new drugs — an objection an honest supporter would have to weigh [S2].

Expanding the acceptable bioequivalence tests beyond absorption studies could raise questions about whether generics approved on alternative evidence are therapeutically interchangeable for all patients, especially for drugs where small differences matter [S2][S3].
The bill did not address drug prices for products still under valid patents, so its help was limited to the moment a legitimate patent expires [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the balance was heavily favorable: generic drugs typically sell for far less than brand versions, and the bill targeted procedural tactics rather than legitimate patent rights — it applied only prospectively, leaving existing applications alone. The main cost was a somewhat weaker incentive for marginal brand-side patenting and research, a trade-off generic-access advocates considered well worth making.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2000, referred to the House Commerce Committee and then its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and sat there while the session ran out, never reaching a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Baldacci, a Maine Democrat, introduced the bill on September 21, 2000, together with Rep. Tom Coburn, an Oklahoma Republican physician [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce [S5].
On October 20, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where no further action occurred [S5].
The bill attracted six cosponsors — five Democrats and one Republican — but the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with no markup or vote [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off, because the tools this bill would have curtailed — ancillary patent listings, delay petitions, and first-filer exclusivity games — remained in place, and consumers kept paying brand prices longer.

for.name: Rep. John Baldacci
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to speed generic drug approval and cut prescription costs.

for.name: Rep. Tom Coburn
for.what_they_did: Joined Baldacci in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 6 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill in its first weeks.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce (106th Congress)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Thomas Bliley (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; after subcommittee referral on October 20, 2000, no markup, hearing, or vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic sponsor joined by a Republican physician, with cosponsors split 5 Democrats to 1 Republican — so the bill died from inaction, not from a party-line fight.

industries.note: The bill narrowed the patents they could cite to block generics, curbed delay petitions, and closed first-filer exclusivity tactics — all tools that extend brand-price sales after the core patent expires. Their loss was consumers' price savings.
Faster, clearer approval paths and accelerated 180-day exclusivity turnover would let generics reach the market sooner, and their cheaper products pass savings to patients and payers.
